Let’s dive into Chapter 7: Overcoming Common Barriers to Brevity.
Even when you set out to keep things brief, sticking to concise communication isn’t always easy. Old habits sneak in, the way things have always been done at work can take over, and sometimes there’s that nagging fear—what if you leave out something important?
Here’s the thing: recognizing these barriers is the first step to making brevity a lasting habit.
One of the biggest obstacles? Believing that longer messages sound more thoughtful or carry more weight. But the truth is, when you pile on the words, it usually just means you’re not as clear as you could be—or maybe you haven’t sorted out your thoughts yet.
Another common trap is trying to cover every possible angle. Ever find yourself explaining too much, just in case? That often leads to information overload and can leave people unsure about what to do next.
So, how do you get past these roadblocks?
First, embrace imperfection. Not every detail needs to make the cut. Ask yourself: what’s truly essential here? Focus on that, and let the rest go.
Second, trust your audience. If they need more info, they’ll ask for it. You don’t have to anticipate every question in advance.
Third, try setting time or word limits. These little boundaries force you to get clear and disciplined about what really matters.
And finally, practice active listening. Notice when people start to lose interest or ask you to repeat yourself. Those are signals that it’s time to simplify.
Here’s something else to consider. Brevity isn’t just about taking shortcuts. It’s actually a way to show respect. When you make your messages clear and easy to grasp, you’re letting people know you value their time and attention.
In the workplace, leaders can help set this tone by celebrating concise communication—and gently steering conversations back on track if they start to wander. Over time, these small changes add up, and brevity becomes the norm, not the exception.
So, the next time you’re tempted to add just one more detail, pause and remember: clear, focused messages go a long way in making your communication more effective—and more appreciated.
